parts.label: Part 3
parts.article:
Section three.

You will hear two psychology students, called Katie and Daniel, discussing how taking a walk can affect people's creativity and physical well-being.

First, you have some time to look at questions twenty-one to twenty-six on page five.

Now listen carefully and answer questions twenty-one to twenty-six.

Hi, Daniel.

Katie, you look as if you're off somewhere.

Yes, I was just heading out for a walk.

Hmm, funny. I was just reading an article about some research that's been done on the effects of walking on creativity.

Huh, sounds interesting.

I've always found walking helped me think, but this article confirms that everybody can benefit.

Oh, tell me more.

Okay, but I may even do some more research on it at some point, so don't pinch my idea.

[giggling] Promise.

[giggling] Well, in the experiments, the researchers tested participants' creativity by comparing how many ideas they thought of while they were walking compared to while they were doing other activities.

What, like listening to music?

Nothing like that. But they did analyze the ideas participants came up with when sitting, both outdoors and inside. What I found surprising was that they didn't compare walking to other forms of exercise, like running, for example.

Right. So what was the difference between the experiments?

Well, in each one, the activities were put together in different ways. Several of the experiments specifically focused on the ability of participants to come up with new ideas. Then the final experiment was a controlled test of sorts.

Oh, right.

In one experiment, participants had to think of unusual uses for three everyday objects within a time limit.

Okay.

And then there was an experiment with words.

What did they ask them to do?

Compare words in unusual ways. For example, the word sweet. If participants simply said, "Sweet as sugar," that wasn't creative. But an answer like, "Sweet as a cat with honey on its paws," was.

Okay. I can see why they'd ask them to do that.

Really? I just don't see how the experiment is fair.

Why? Because the conclusions are based only on the researcher's opinion?

I think it's more that anyone who'd studied language would be at an advantage.

Hmm, okay. Was there an experiment about focused thinking?

Yeah, there was. It aimed to find out if walking helped focused thinking, though I wasn't sure that I agreed with their findings. They decided that walking doesn't help this type of thinking.

What evidence did they have?

Well, that's it. I don't think there was enough evidence to support their conclusions, even if their methods were sound.

Well, I'd certainly hesitate before making such a bold statement.

Still, it's a first step, isn't it? I suppose to move forward with this, they'll need to test other ways people keep fit, like swimming.

That would be useful, but personally, I'd like to know more about the fundamental reason for the effect on people's creativity.

That would be good. Then it could be applied more widely in work, for example.

Again, that's secondary, really.

Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions twenty-seven to thirty on page six.

Now listen and answer questions twenty-seven to thirty.

But how would you test walking if you wanted to assess its physical benefits?

Well, firstly, I'd like to know more about the benefits of different situations.

What about the effect of footwear?

Hmm, hadn't thought of that.

Well, I've read that shoes with thinner soles were found to be better for people's joints. It even made the skeletal structure tougher.

Interesting. Was that because they lost weight?

Not as far as I'm aware. And then there's walking in the mountains.

Walking in the mountains. Hmm, I think I've read something about that. Doesn't altitude help people regulate their sleep patterns?

Mm, it's more that it improves your vision.

It must be those breathtaking views.

Yeah. [giggling]

And what about the effect that walking has for elderly people?

Better balance, by any chance?

More than that. It had a positive effect by helping them maintain their body clock's natural rhythm, both when going to bed and waking up.

Right. And what about the effect of walking long distances?

Well, a person needs to find the balance between their optimum speed and their natural breathing pattern. Once they're synchronized, they can just keep on going for much longer periods than they could before.

Hmm. I can see how that would work. But anyway...

That is the end of Section three. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

questions.question: In the experiments, researchers compared participants’ creativity when walking and when

analyses.content: 录音明确提到研究人员分析了参与者在“坐着（sitting）”时想出的点子，以此来和散步进行对比。
你可能会听到 music 和 running 的干扰，但录音明确否定了听音乐（Nothing like that），并表示很惊讶他们“没有（didn't）”拿跑步来做对比，千万别漏听否定词。

Well, in the experiments, the researchers tested participants' creativity by comparing how many ideas they thought of while they were walking compared to while they were doing other activities. What, like listening to music? Nothing like that. But they did analyze the ideas participants came up with when sitting, both outdoors and inside. What I found surprising was that they didn't compare walking to other forms of exercise, like running, for example.

questions.question: Daniel says that in each experiment, there was a different

analyses.content: 当被问到实验之间有什么不同时，Daniel直接回答说每项实验中“活动的组合方式不同（activities were put together in different ways）”，对应选项中的活动模式（pattern of activities）。
你可能会因为没跟上 activities 这个词的同义转述而陷入犹豫，注意识别 put together in different ways 其实就是在表达 pattern（模式/组合）。
Right. So what was the difference between the experiments? Well, in each one, the activities were put together in different ways.

analyses.content: 面对未来的研究方向，Katie明确强调她个人最想了解的是影响创造力的“根本原因（fundamental reason）”，完美对应选项中的 cause。
A选项（测试其他运动）和C选项（应用到工作中）都是Daniel提出的建议，且C选项更是被Katie当场反驳为“次要的（secondary）”，审题时要死死盯住问的是“Katie”的观点。

Walking situations
27 Walking with thin-soled footwear
28 Walking in the mountains
29 Walking for the elderly
30 Walking long distances

analyses.content: 录音明确指出，鞋底较薄的鞋子能让“骨骼结构更坚固（skeletal structure tougher）”，直接对应选项中的“骨骼更强壮（stronger bones）”。
你可能会先听到 better for people's joints 而想去找跟关节相关的答案，但最终结论落在紧接着的下一句“骨骼结构更坚固”上，要听到完整的语义结束。
What about the effect of footwear? Hmm, hadn't thought of that. Well, I've read that shoes with thinner soles were found to be better for people's joints. It even made the skeletal structure tougher.
Daniel直接否定了之前的猜测，给出确切结论：在山地行走能“改善视力（improves your vision）”，对应 better eyesight。
女生Katie抛出了“调节睡眠模式（sleep patterns）”作为干扰，你很容易顺手选了E，必须听出后面男声对其进行的纠正信息。

Walking in the mountains. Hmm, I think I've read something about that. Doesn't altitude help people regulate their sleep patterns? Mm, it's more that it improves your vision. It must be those breathtaking views.
录音说明散步能帮助老年人维持“生物钟的自然节律（body clock's natural rhythm）”，无论是睡觉还是起床，这就对应了规律的睡眠模式（regular sleeping pattern）。
Katie用疑问句抛出了“更好的平衡（Better balance）”这个强干扰，你如果只抓取关键词很容易错选A，要注意男声回答的“More than that”意味着后面的才是核心答案。

And what about the effect that walking has for elderly people? Better balance, by any chance? More than that. It had a positive effect by helping them maintain their body clock's natural rhythm, both when going to bed and waking up.
录音解释说，一旦速度和呼吸同步，人们就能“坚持更长的时间（keep on going for much longer periods）”，这就是耐力（stamina）增强的直接体现。
你可能会听到 balance 就急着想选A，但这里的 balance 是指寻找速度和呼吸之间的平衡，其最终导致的身体益处是“能走得更久”，切忌听到什么选什么。

And what about the effect of walking long distances? Well, a person needs to find the balance between their optimum speed and their natural breathing pattern. Once they're synchronized, they can just keep on going for much longer periods than they could before.
